articles.summary: U.S.-China Report 2026 Fall Update angela.wan+a Tue, 10/20/2026 - 12:03 Download this report Watch the seminar video in English Separating Macro Re-AI-lities from Macro Fant-AI-sies Artificial intelligence has not overtaken every corner of the economy, but it dominates the current economic conversation as though it has. While not unprecedented, it is rare for a single technology to capture the country’s zeitgeist so completely. Stock market concentration offers one measure of just how pervasive the AI narrative is. The ten most AI-exposed companies now account for around 40 percent of total U.S. stock market value, according to Bank of America Global Investment Strategy, a share that rivals the peaks reached by the Nifty Fifty in 1972, Japan’s bubble-era conglomerates in 1989, and the dot-com bubble of 1999 (Figure 1a). Unfortunately, a bigger investment boom doesn’t always signal a bigger breakthrough. Plotting peak investment as a share of GDP against each technology’s estimated long-run contribution to productivity growth across six historical episodes produces a relationship that is only faintly positive (Figure 1b)1. However, we would caution against drawing any strong conclusions from six episodes, each measured with wide errors. While boom size has been a weak guide to the growth that follows it, larger booms do tend to fund more of the underlying infrastructure that the technology eventually requires. A study from the Bank for International Settlements characterizes the technology buildout as a contest among a handful of firms racing for a small number of dominant positions. This is the same competitive dynamic that pushed prior technologies toward overbuilt infrastructure along with excessive financial fragility. Each firm, rational on its own, over-commits resources to avoid being shut out of a market that may only support a few winners. Their study puts the resulting over-investment at 1.5 to 3 times the efficient level. The same competitive logic that produces the overbuilding also produces the uncertain but potentially large payoff to whichever firm wins the race, which is what keeps capital flowing in even after the overbuilding becomes apparent to everyone in the contest. The times therefore call for an assessment of what impact artificial intelligence is currently having, and not having, on the U.S. macroeconomy. We split the discussion into two parts, one assessing AI’s impact on the macro-financial system, the other on the labor market. Figure 1a. Today’s AI concentration mirrors every prior tech mania Figure 1b. Buildout size tells us little about the payoff The Macro-financial System What are the current financial realities, and fantasies, surrounding AI? One of the key metrics for assessing whether equity markets are over- or undervalued is the cyclically adjusted price-earnings ratio, or CAPE. Currently above 40, CAPE is near the level it reached at the peak of the dot-com bubble (Figure 2a). Andrew Atkeson, Jonathan Heathcote, and Fabrizio Perri offer a structural explanation. They argue that valuation ratios have risen above their historical norms over the past 30 years because labor’s share of corporate output has declined while corporate investment has remained relatively weak, which mechanically raises the value of corporations relative to their earnings. Because free cash flow, defined as earnings minus net investment, rose in step with enterprise value from 1980 to mid-2022, the ratio of free cash flow to enterprise value held steady over that period, unlike the standard earnings-based ratio. Today, the cyclically adjusted price to free cash flow ratio, or CAPC, is around 54, against an average of 37 over 1961–2019 and above 80 on average in 2000, at the height of the dot-com boom. Relative to their 1961–2019 averages, the cash-flow multiple has risen by far less than the earnings-based one, about 50 percent above its average against roughly double for CAPE, and its current level, while high, is nowhere near its dot-com peak. However, this is changing as free cash flow at the largest technology firms has begun to fall sharply in 2026, as they shift from capital-light to capital-heavy operations. The measure rises by construction during investment booms, since heavy capital spending depresses free cash flow whether or not that spending eventually pays off. That is part of why the dot-com reading was so extreme. Combined free cash flow at the four largest hyperscalers came to $199 billion in 2025. It fell to $20 billion in the first quarter of 2026 and $7 billion in the second, an annualized rate near $30 billion, with Amazon and Alphabet’s turning negative (Figure 2b). If this pace of spending continues, the free cash flow cushion that made high valuations defensible will begin to disappear, and the CAPC valuation will drift further upwards relative to CAPE. Figure 2a. On cash flow, valuations are the highest outside the dot-com era Figure 2b. AI capex has eroded Big Tech’s cash flow There are also signs that at least some corners of financial markets have stopped pricing AI exposure on economic fundamentals. The skew in S&P 500 options , a measure of how much more investors pay for protection against a sharp decline than for exposure to a comparable rally, recently fell to its lowest level since mid-2024, according to Cboe. In other words, investors are betting on further upside about as enthusiastically as they are hedging against a downturn, which is unusual, especially for a market already trading at high valuations. It might suggest a concerning level of complacency and a lack of careful risk pricing. An illustration of this complacency unwinding came in July 2026, when Leopold Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness fund, built on highly concentrated AI bets, suffered a sell-off that now ranks as the largest trading loss in history , to the tune of $35 billion. Meanwhile, Allbirds, a shoe company, rebranded itself as NewBird AI in 2026 in a shift to GPU cloud computing. Its stock price surged as much as 600 percent on the announcement, adding roughly $127 million in market capitalization within a day. The timing of the current IPO pipeline of SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI is in part based on this investor enthusiasm. Bringing a company public is as much a question of timing the market as it is of outgrowing what private capital is able to fund. In South Korea, retail investors piled into single-stock leveraged exchange-traded funds tracking SK Hynix and Samsung as the two chipmakers benefited from the AI-driven boom in memory-chip demand. Combined assets in those leveraged funds swelled to roughly ₩31 trillion (about $20 billion) by their June 2026 peak, and by early July, the leveraged funds together with the two underlying stocks accounted for roughly 70 percent of all trading value on the Korean stock market (Figure 3a). The bubble then popped, with the primary Korean stock index, the Kospi, falling 44 percent from its June high. Combined leveraged-ETF trading volume collapsed by roughly 90 percent within about a week of new trading curbs taking effect, and assets in the leveraged funds are down by roughly two-thirds from their June peak. This event is a classic illustration of how leverage can turn a real trade, the AI memory-chip boom, into a bubble. Credit markets are beginning to signal some warning regarding the current financial excesses. Big Tech credit default swap spreads have widened as the companies take on debt to fund the buildout. Oracle’s five-year CDS spread is the starkest example, surpassing the peak it reached during the financial crisis of 2008–09 (Figure 3b). Figure 3a. Korea’s single-stock leverage bubble inflated and burst Figure 3b. Markets now price Oracle as riskier than in the 2008–09 crisis Are these financial metrics warranted? Are we headed for an unprecedented boom, bust, or something more mundane? Answering this means setting the market narrative aside and asking what the underlying macroeconomic realities and fantasies actually are in relation to AI. Capital Expenditures Combined capex among the seven largest AI builders has climbed from $160 billion in 2022, where it stayed through 2023, to a projected $863 billion in 2026. These figures imply some remarkable growth rates of 68 percent in 2024, 71 percent in 2025, and 88 percent in 2026 (Figure 4a). This pace of growth is neither likely nor expected to continue. Big Tech firms have mostly stopped revising their investment plans upward, and their guidance points to growth decelerating in 2027 as annual spending is set to surpass one trillion dollars and increasingly outrun their own free cash flow. Goldman Sachs’s credit strategists put the share of hyperscaler capital spending financed by debt at 27 percent in 2025 and roughly a third in 2026, peaking near 35 percent in 2027. They also count close to $500 billion of AI-related debt issuance, of which the hyperscalers account for only 40 percent, with the rest raised by borrowers who have considerably smaller balance sheets. This trillion-dollar buildout is not hard to spot in the construction and investment data, both in quantities and prices (Figure 4b). Private data-center construction spending, measured in constant dollars, swung from an early, small-base boom and bust in 2015–19 to a sustained climb since 2023, peaking near 84 percent year-over-year growth in mid-2024 and cooling to around 20 percent by the spring of 2026. It has reaccelerated since, to 28 percent in June on a three-month average basis and 44 percent in the month of June alone. Business investment in computers and peripheral equipment has followed an even steeper recent path. It was up 75 percent year-over-year in the fourth quarter of 2025, 72 percent in the first quarter of 2026, and 58 percent in the second. Prices for that same equipment, which historically decline over time, have jumped sharply in the last few months, to 23 percent year-over-year in August, likely reflecting the broader AI-driven memory-chip shortage now passing through into finished computer-equipment prices. Figure 4a. Cash flows are now insufficient to fund the buildout Figure 4b. The buildout is both a volume and price boom AI-related investment in software and information-processing equipment, together with the AI-driven wealth effect on consumption described below, accounted for nearly half of core GDP growth over the year through the second quarter of 2026 (Figure 5a)2. Stripping that contribution out, and disregarding any crowding-out effects it has had, the remaining economy has been growing noticeably more slowly than the headline figures suggest. Earnings growth The revenues attributable to AI are growing fast. The current run-rate revenue across the major AI providers is somewhere between $150 and $217.5 billion on The Economist ’s account. Cumulative AI infrastructure capex among the seven largest builders since 2022 amounts to about $1.9 trillion (Figure 4a). Recovering this capital over a (generous) six-year depreciation schedule at a 10 percent required rate of return costs about $440 billion a year. Epoch AI’s estimate that electricity, cooling, bandwidth and staff make up about a tenth of the annual total cost of ownership of a one-gigawatt facility puts the full annual cost of the buildout near $500 billion. J.P. Morgan Asset Management puts the revenue required for a 10 percent return nearer $650 billion a year. AI revenues are thus short by a factor of two to four. Revenues have been growing rapidly, however. Epoch AI finds that combined revenue at OpenAI and Anthropic tripled in 2024, more than quadrupled in 2025, and has grown 3.5-fold so far in 2026. Even if total industry revenues only double each year, this hurdle may be within reach in a few years. But capex continues to grow as well, raising the hurdle at the same time. The broader pattern of strong corporate earnings growth in the US is not itself an AI story. Reporting in the Wall Street Journal has traced a meaningful share of 2026’s corporate profit growth to tariff refunds and to investment gains on the equity stakes held by Amazon and Alphabet, rather than to AI-driven productivity gains. AI equity valuation gains have also boosted consumer spending, thereby supporting corporate earnings growth. Household holdings of corporate equities and mutual-fund shares rose from $34 trillion at the end of 2022 to $56 trillion at the end of 2025. Attributing half of that $22 trillion gain to AI, and applying a marginal propensity to consume out of wealth of 4 percent, raises the level of consumer spending by about $450 billion by the end of 2025, or roughly $150 billion a year of additional spending over the three years. This spending amounts to about a quarter of the growth in real consumption and a fifth of real GDP growth, which is about half a percentage point of GDP a year (Figure 5a). That is a meaningful but fragile contribution to aggregate growth. It depends on AI-related equity valuations continuing to hold at a moment when the personal saving rate has been hovering at or below 3 percent. Circular financing Robin Brooks decomposed the U.S. sectoral saving-investment balance to show that corporations are currently running as net savers rather than net borrowers. This is a sharp contrast with the corporate sector’s position during the dot-com bubble and a reflection of the profitability of the hyperscalers currently funding much of the buildout (Figure 5b). Up to 2025, this boom remained mostly self-funded by highly profitable companies rather than mostly financed by external debt the way the telecom buildout of the late 1990s was. The funding has begun to shift toward debt financing as mentioned above (Figure 4a). Moreover, much of AI financing has grown increasingly off-balance-sheet, routed through future spending commitments and vendor-financing arrangements that do not show up neatly in any single company’s reported leverage. The Wall Street Journal counts around $3 trillion of off-balance-sheet commitments at nine large technology companies. There is a concern that a meaningful amount of hidden risk is being built up in the financial system. Figure 5a. AI now drives nearly half of core GDP growth Figure 5b. This boom isn’t financed the way the dot-com boom was Nvidia is at the center of this financing structure, as it is both the industry’s dominant supplier and, increasingly, one of its principal financiers. The Financial Times puts Nvidia’s balance-sheet exposure across these arrangements near $200 billion once contingent and off-balance-sheet commitments are counted. Circular financing of this kind is not inherently unsound. A supplier with a strong balance sheet extending credit to its customers is a familiar feature of capital-intensive industries. But it does mean that a disappointment in AI demand could lead to a much larger unraveling, and the chip industry, which is currently financing this one, is notoriously cyclical. The Labor Market Overall employment growth has slowed to a trickle, and technology hiring in particular has gone from boom to bust since 2022, but neither of these patterns requires an AI explanation. Software-development job postings, tracked by Indeed , are in fact recovering, up roughly 20 percent from their 2025 trough even as overall job postings have drifted down (Figure 6a). Technology firms hired aggressively during the post-pandemic boom, and the pullback since has been, to a considerable degree, a correction of that overhiring. That boom was partly due to the near-zero interest rate environment at the time, and the Federal Reserve’s subsequent rate increases were widely expected to tip the economy into recession in 2023. That recession never arrived, but the tightening was sufficient to cool the labor market meaningfully. Overall employment growth is unusually low, though this appears to be driven mainly by immigration and demographic trends. Employment cannot grow if the labor force is not growing when the economy is at full employment. Youth hiring has also fallen by more than what a standard business-cycle fluctuation would predict. The junior share of new hires now sits 8 to 11 percentage points below its 2019 level across the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia (Figure 6b). New business formation has also recently shifted to a higher rate, and it is being driven disproportionately by non-employer businesses. Solo business applications are up more than 20 percent since early 2025 , while applications from prospective employers have been broadly flat. Close to half of the increase in solo applications has come from technology, finance, and professional services, the sectors where AI adoption is highest. Figure 6a. Software hiring is climbing again after a brutal bust Figure 6b. Junior hiring has collapsed across Anglophone economies What can be attributed to AI? There is already no shortage of studies attempting to assess the effect that AI is having on the labor market. Collectively, they can support almost any narrative one wants to believe3. The findings that have gained the most traction are the potential effects that AI has had on reducing junior hiring and inhibiting wage growth of those occupations most exposed to it. Few individual studies are more than suggestive in one direction or the other. At this point, there is certainly no conclusive evidence of a large AI impact on the labor market. Part of the disagreement has to do with the measurement of AI exposure and AI adoption. There is no single, agreed-upon way to measure an occupation’s exposure to AI, and whether that exposure is one that augments or displaces it. Because of this, there is a plethora of different measures that do not always agree with one another. Apollo’s Torsten Sløk created a compilation of exposure studies showing that disagreement is larger when exposure estimates are higher (Figure 7). AI adoption measures also disagree, as the St. Louis Fed points out. They range widely, depending on who is surveyed and how the question is worded. When the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey changed its own question wording in November 2025, from whether a business had used AI in producing goods or services to whether it had used AI in any of its business functions, the measured adoption rate stepped up from about 10 percent to about 17 percent in a single month. Adoption rises to 37 percent among larger firms, but even adopting firms still typically use AI to supplement only a small number of business functions rather than to restructure how the business operates. The reason businesses most often give for not adopting is that they do not think AI applies to their business. Figure 7. The more AI-exposed the job, the less studies agree Further muddying the waters is the practice of AI washing, in which corporations attribute layoffs to AI for public-relations reasons. In a Resume.org survey of 1,000 hiring managers fielded in December 2025, 59 percent admitted to playing up AI’s role in layoffs and hiring freezes because the narrative sits better with stakeholders than an admission of financial strain, while only 9 percent said AI had actually replaced roles at their firm. Challenger, Gray & Christmas data , which attributed 54,836 announced job cuts in 2025 to AI against only 7,908 to tariffs, should thus be read with that incentive in mind. It is also worth keeping the scale of individual layoff announcements in perspective. Something on the order of 1.7 million layoffs happen every month in the United States in the ordinary course of business, which means any single company’s job-cut announcement, however prominently covered by the media, is rarely informative about the economy-wide pattern. What does remote work have to do with AI? The shift to working from home accelerated sharply during the pandemic, before generative AI tools began appearing. Remote work makes coaching and supervising junior employees harder, leading to reductions in junior hiring through a similar mechanism that is often attributed to AI. Consistent with that account, Lambert and Schindler find that the occupations most exposed to remote work turn out to be the same occupations most exposed to generative AI (Figure 8a). The shift to remote work also fits the timing better than the introduction of generative AI, with the decline in early-career postings beginning around 2020. More importantly, once remote-work exposure is controlled for, AI exposure no longer predicts a significant decline in early-career job postings (or hiring), while the remote-work effect remains present when controlling for AI (Figure 8b). Figure 8a. WFH and GenAI exposure are highly correlated across occupations Figure 8b. Remote work, not AI, tracks the decline in early-career postings The work of Gregor Schubert , here at UCLA Anderson, adds another layer of nuance that does not require picking a winner between whether remote work or AI is inhibiting junior hiring. Schubert shows that remote-work adoption itself drives firms’ later AI adoption. Firms that hired remotely in 2021 and 2022 shifted toward technical and managerial talent, and that capability lowered the cost of adopting generative AI in 2023 and 2024, with a ten-percentage-point increase in remote hiring predicting a 0.4 to 0.7 percentage-point rise in AI adoption. If remote work sits upstream of AI adoption, the two are not competing explanations at all but successive rungs on the same ladder, climbed by the same technology-forward firms. Controlling for remote work, as Lambert and Schindler do, would then absorb part of the channel through which AI affects junior hiring. Productivity growth AI is expected to induce anywhere from modest to unprecedented gains in productivity. Measured against the historical relationship between GDP growth and employment growth, the current expansion is only producing marginally more output per unit of job growth than the 1948–2019 average would predict (Figure 9a). Against the depressed productivity growth of the 2010s, this is an improvement, but against the full sweep of postwar history, it looks more like a normalization. There is hope that the economy is on a trajectory similar to that of the late-1990s productivity boom, though so far it is a softer version of it. The economy now sits about 0.4 percentage points above the historical relationship, against roughly 0.8 in late 1999, and with substantially less employment growth. The most recent rise in productivity does not appear to be coming from AI either. Boyle, Fernald, and Li of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco show that since the beginning of 2024, and across 2025 and 2026, higher capacity utilization accounts for essentially all of the growth in total factor productivity, meaning firms are running their existing capital and labor harder rather than becoming more efficient at converting inputs into output in any fundamental sense (Figure 9b). Across 2025 and 2026, utilization-adjusted total factor productivity has been slightly negative even as measured productivity growth stayed positive, a much less encouraging story than the headline numbers suggest. Figure 9a. Today’s productivity run echoes the late-1990s boom Figure 9b. The productivity surge is utilization, not fundamental gains Chad Syverson , among the most prominent economists studying productivity, reaches a similar conclusion in his 2026 report, finding no clear evidence that AI is yet moving aggregate productivity. He notes a timing problem for anyone eager to credit AI with the recent uptick. The acceleration began when AI investment was still small relative to the economy, which leans against AI having been its initial cause. However, he does note that even if something else started the acceleration, AI could well be contributing now. If we are willing to ignore the retail sector, higher AI adoption (as measured by the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey) does loosely line up with larger productivity gains across sectors. The admitted tenuousness of his results underlines one of the main takeaways of this report, which is that it is simply still too soon to make any concrete statement regarding the effects of AI. However, the longer elevated productivity growth persists, the more plausible an AI contribution becomes. Conclusion None of this should be read as an argument that AI will fail to transform the economy, and the labor market with it. At the time of this writing, however, while the buildout and financing of AI are having large effects on the macroeconomy, the impact of the technology itself remains marginal to non-existent. When more conclusive evidence arrives, which the economists here at UCLA Anderson Forecast expect it eventually will, we will address it. This may not happen quickly, as new general-purpose technologies have historically taken a long time to be productively absorbed into the economy. AI may move faster than its predecessors given how quickly the underlying tools are already diffusing, but by the evidence available today, we remain at the very beginning of this economic transformation. articles.summary: You leave the hotel with a few stops in mind. By lunch, you've found a bookstore, taken more photos than expected, and decided the market across town is worth the walk. A good sightseeing bag can keep up with that kind of day. The best day bag for sightseeing gives you enough room for what you want to bring along, keeps the things you need easy to find, and feels right with what you're wearing. Here's how to choose one for the way you like to explore. Best Bag for an All-Day Itinerary When you'll be out from morning until dinner, start with what you actually plan to bring. A wallet and phone are one thing. Add a small umbrella, sunglasses, a snack, and the little things you collect throughout the day, and pockets become much more useful. Small Banbury Backpack: Room to Stay Organized The Small Banbury Backpack is a good compact bag for day trip plans that cover a lot of ground. Its adjustable straps leave your hands free for maps, photos, and whatever you pick up along the way. An exterior zip compartment keeps frequently used items separate from the main compartment, while two side pockets let you bring a water bottle or compact umbrella. Dimensions: 7" w, 11.75" h, 4.75" d "Super cute pattern and I love the lightweight material! Love the size for travel and love that you can still fit a water bottle in the side!" ~ Lauren Lorman Sling Backpack: A Lighter Way to Roam The Lorman Sling Backpack has a narrower shape for days when you're carrying less. Its convertible strap lets you wear it over your left or right shoulder, so you can choose what feels comfortable as you move through the city. Two exterior zip compartments give essentials their own spots, with a back slip pocket and a slip pocket in the main compartment to stash your phone, wallet and more. It's a great choice when you want the ease of a backpack in a slimmer style. Dimensions: 6.5" w, 11" h, 2.75" d "Very sturdy and stylish, holds just enough for a day trip or traveling." ~ Margaret Best Bag for Hands-Free Exploring A crossbody makes sense when the day involves walking, browsing, and moving between activities. How much you bring will help you decide whether you want a compact bag or more space. Becker Camera Bag Crossbody: Just the Essentials The Becker Camera Bag Crossbody is for the traveler who knows what she needs and brings exactly that. Its compact shape measures 8.25" wide, 5.5" high, and 3" deep, so it's an easy choice for a few hours of sightseeing or an evening out. A front zip pocket and back slip pocket give you places for items you reach for often; inside, two slip pockets and a zip pocket help keep your phone, wallet, keys, and small necessities in order. The adjustable strap lets you settle it where you like, and the zip closure keeps the main compartment secure between stops. Dimensions: 8.25" w, 5.5" h, and 3" d "Small, but holds the essentials I need. Love the wide strap as it sits comfortably on my shoulder." ~ Nancy Harwick Large Messenger: More Room, Same Freedom If you prefer a crossbody but want one that holds more, look to the Harwick Large Messenger bag. Its structured silhouette adds a polished touch to an outfit, while its generous size gives you more room than a compact camera bag. Harwick's front zip pocket has two slip pockets inside, handy when you want to find small items without opening the main compartment. Two back slip pockets add quick-access storage, and an interior zip pocket and two slip pockets help organize what you carry inside. It's a strong contender for the best bag for city sightseeing when your plans take you from morning coffee to an afternoon museum and on to dinner. Dimensions: 11.5" w x 11.0" h x 3.5" d "Hands free and large enough to carry whatever you may need for any occasion. Enough pockets too to make it easy to find everything." ~ Rita Best Bag for Carrying Layers, Snacks, and Souvenirs Some itineraries practically invite you to bring something home. If you're visiting markets, stopping in shops, or carrying a few extra items for the kids, a tote or roomier handbag can make more sense than a small crossbody. Check the dimensions against what you plan to carry, especially for bulkier layers or purchases. Small Original Vera Tote: A Little Extra Room Our Small Original Vera Tote is a petite version of a familiar favorite. Its clean shape works for a museum day or a market visit, while the zip closure helps keep everything together as you move between stops. Six interior slip pockets give your smaller essentials places to land, so they're easier to find when you need them. An exterior slip pocket and zip pocket add options for the things you want to reach quickly. That shape gives you some flexibility for the day's extras without asking you to carry a full-size tote. Dimensions: 11.5" h, 4.5" d, 11.5" w at its base, with a wider 16.25" opening at the top "Love the design and size. My go to purse for traveling and carrying a good book to read with me!" ~ Katrina Hathaway Reversible Tote Bag: Space and Style Options When you want maximum flexibility, step up to the Hathaway Reversible Tote Bag. It's a large capacity tote bag that's easy to carry thanks to the comfortable 12” handle drop. As an added bonus, the bag is fully reversible so you can match any outfit or occasion on your trip. No matter which side you choose, an exterior slip pocket keeps your phone and necessities easy to reach while an interior slip pocket gives an extra option for organization. The unstructured style can fit a few items secured with a hidden magnetic closure, or leave the top open for those bigger shopping finds and travel take-alongs. Dimensions: 13.0" h x 6.25" d, 13.75" w at its base, with a wider 20.5" opening at the top "Perfect size for a quick trip out shopping. Love the style." ~ Teresa Best Bag for a Day That Runs Into Dinner Sightseeing plans have a way of growing. If you'd rather keep the same bag for an afternoon of wandering and dinner afterward, choose one that fits how you want to carry it. Original 100 Handbag: The Vera Bradley Classic The Original 100 Handbag brings Vera Bradley's original silhouette along for the trip. The most organized shoulder bag you'll ever have, it features three exterior slip pockets and five interior slip pockets. This is a particularly welcome detail when you've gathered receipts, tickets, sunglasses, and the other small traces of a day well spent. Its quilted cotton lining and familiar shape give it a character all its own. With a zip closure and 13.5" handle drop, it's a lovely choice for someone who wants a classic handbag that you can throw over your shoulder comfortably. Dimensions: 11.0" w x 5.75" h x 5.5" d "This is a great bag, handles are long enough to put on your shoulder with a coat on. The Small Original Vera Tote and Original 100 Handbag suit days with extra stops and a few finds; Clara moves easily into evening plans.
